title: Muslim women's voices
hook: Muslim women speak for themselves on dress, work, scholarship and faith, and they don't all agree

segments.voice: Yesterday, converts and reverts. Your line: new to it. Did you do the small welcoming thing for someone new? Today, voices best heard in their own words. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-seven.

A woman comes to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, with a complaint about her husband. He has spoken an old pagan formula over her, and by the custom of the time it means she is cut off from him, neither married nor free. She argues her case. She doesn't let it drop. She turns her complaint to Allah. And the surah that opens with her story is named for her argument: al-Mujadila, she who disputes. Its first verse says that Allah has heard the woman who pleaded with the Prophet about her husband. Her name, tradition says, was Khawlah. A chapter of scripture begins by listening to a woman speak.
screen: `SHE ARGUES HER CASE.` → `AL-MUJADILA: SHE WHO DISPUTES.` → `ALLAH HAS HEARD HER.`

segments.voice: First, the early voices. Khawlah wasn't alone. Tradition says Umm Salamah, the Prophet's wife, asked why the Qur'an spoke of men and not of women, and that a verse in surah al-Ahzab came down naming both, in Pickthall's words: "Lo! men who surrender unto Allah, and women who surrender, and men who believe and women who believe". And 'A'ishah became a teacher whom companions consulted. In a report kept in Sahih Muslim, she praises the women of the Ansar, saying, in paraphrase, that shyness didn't keep them from learning their religion. Second, the scholars. Tradition remembers women who narrated hadith and taught it, with men among their students. That line of women teaching continues in schools and mosques today. Third, today's voices, in the plural. Muslim women write on law, run clinics, lead businesses, raise families, recite the Qur'an, preach to women's gatherings, and argue in public. They speak on dress, on work, on mosque space, on scholarship. Fourth, they don't all agree. Some argue from the classical schools and explain their views from there. Some propose fresh readings of the texts. Some wear hijab and some don't, and both groups explain their reasons. Some work outside the home and some choose not to, and give their reasons too. The disagreements happen among Muslim women themselves. Nobody needs an outsider, or a narrator, to settle them. The one thing a listener can do is notice who is speaking. Is it a Muslim woman, in her own words? Or is someone speaking about her?
screen: `KHAWLAH, UMM SALAMAH, 'A'ISHAH.` · `WOMEN TAUGHT, AND MEN LEARNED.` · `MANY VOICES, IN THE PLURAL.` · `THEY DON'T ALL AGREE.`

segments.voice: The practice: listen to a Muslim woman's talk. First, practice the listening itself. Settle, and breathe. Let the sounds around you come and go without naming them. A car. A fan. Your own breath. For a few breaths, just receive, the way the surah begins: someone spoke, and was heard. If you pray, you can ask in your own words for a hearing heart. Later today, find one short talk, lecture or interview by a Muslim woman, a scholar, a writer, anyone, and listen to the end before deciding what you think. The bell holds the time.
Muslim women's voices. From Khawlah and 'A'ishah to scholars and writers today, women speaking for themselves on faith, dress, work and learning, and not always agreeing. Today's word.

Your line: they speak for themselves. Today, when a conversation turns to any group of people, ask whether anyone from that group is in the room. Tomorrow, hijab, many choices. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Muslim women teach in mosques and schools, narrate and study hadith, write and speak on law and faith, and lead women's study circles; they hold a range of views on dress, work and mosque space, and argue for them in their own words.

trapdoor: what you thought: Muslim women are mostly talked about, not heard.
what it means: from Khawlah to scholars today, Muslim women speak for themselves on faith, dress, work and learning, and they don't all agree.
what a scholar hears: a surah named for a woman's plea, Umm Salamah's question behind al-Ahzab, and 'A'ishah's praise of the women of the Ansar who weren't too shy to learn.

notes: Confirm Abu Dawud 2214 (Khawlah), Tirmidhi 3211 (Umm Salamah and 33:35) and Muslim 332 ('A'ishah on the women of the Ansar) numbering.

The hook explains zihar briefly ('an old pagan formula'); confirm the description.
